title: The strict practices
hook: rag robes, alms food, living in the forest: the Buddha tells Kassapa he is old and may let them go, and Kassapa explains why he keeps them (SN 16.5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, exchanging robes: Kassapa gave his soft cloak and took the Buddha's worn rag robes. Your line was the worn robe. What plain thing did you wear or use on purpose? Today, how long he kept wearing it. Day seven hundred forty-one.

The robes are heavy now. That's the first thing the Buddha says in this short discourse. Kassapa has grown old, and the hempen rag robes he's worn for so long hang heavy on him. So the Buddha makes a kind offer. You're old, Kassapa. Wear the robes householders give you. Accept meals when people invite you. Live near me, instead of out in the forest. Nobody would blame him. His teacher is giving him permission. And Kassapa, politely, says no.
screen: `THE ROBES ARE HEAVY NOW.` → `A KIND OFFER.` → `KASSAPA SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: First, what he keeps. In the discourse Kassapa lists his way of life: a long time living in the forest, eating only what he receives on the alms round, wearing rag robes, keeping only the robes he needs, wanting little, content, secluded, putting in effort. And he says he praises these things to others too. Later tradition gathers practices like these under one name, dhutanga. Second, the name. In the Path of Purification, Buddhaghosa's long handbook, these are explained as practices of a monk who has shaken off the defilements. They're not required of anyone. They're chosen, on top of the ordinary rules, by those who want a sharper, simpler life. Third, his reasons. The Buddha asks him why he keeps them, and Kassapa gives two. One: they make for a pleasant life for him, here and now. He isn't suffering through them; he likes living this way. Two, and this is where today's line comes from: compassion for those who come later. He hopes that people in the future will look back and say, the disciples of the Buddha lived like this, and take heart, and try it too. Fourth, the answer. The Buddha says: good, good, Kassapa. You are practicing for the welfare of many people, out of compassion for the world. So an old man keeps carrying heavy robes, not to prove anything, and not because he has to, but so that someone he'll never meet can see that the path is still walked. For those to come.
screen: `FOREST, ALMS, RAG ROBES.` · `PRACTICES OF SHAKING OFF.` · `A PLEASANT LIFE, HERE AND NOW.` · `AN EXAMPLE FOR LATER PEOPLE.` · then, large: `FOR THOSE TO COME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one simple practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small, plain habit you already keep, or once kept. A walk without the phone. Tea without a screen. Making your bed. Eating one meal slowly. Pick one. Now ask Kassapa's two questions about it. Does it make this life a little more pleasant, here and now? And who might see it, a child, a roommate, a friend, and quietly take it up? You don't need a big answer. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Dhutanga. Simple, strict practices, like forest living, alms food and rag robes, taken up by choice; Kassapa keeps them into old age. Today's word.
Your line: for those to come. Today, keep your one simple practice where someone else might see it, and let that be a small gift to whoever comes next. Day seven hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: In the Thai forest tradition and other Theravada communities, some monks take up dhutanga practices for a time or for life, such as eating one meal a day from the alms round or living in the forest, while others keep only the ordinary rules.

fork.setup: you're Kassapa, old, and your teacher kindly offers to let you live an easier life. what do you do?
options: keep the strict practices, and explain why.
accept, but keep one practice in secret.
fork.reveal: he keeps them, for his own pleasant life and as an example for those to come, and the Buddha approves.

original.note: Pali dhutanga: the practices of one who shakes off defilements, in the Path of Purification's explanation.

trapdoor: what you thought: harsh rules for punishing the body.
what it means: simple practices taken up by choice, which Kassapa calls a pleasant life and an example for others.
what a scholar hears: the word dhutanga isn't in SN 16.5; the Path of Purification later gathers these practices under that name and explains it.
recall: takes the rules like a garland

notes: SN 16.5 paraphrased; confirm the list of Kassapa's practices (forest dweller, alms-food eater, rag-robe wearer, three-robe wearer, few wishes, content, secluded, aloof, energetic) and that he 'speaks in praise' of them, the two reasons, and the Buddha's approval ('for the welfare of many people, out of compassion for the world').
Explanation of 'dhutanga' as practices of one who has 'shaken off' defilements is attributed to the Visuddhimagga (ch. 2); confirm. The number of dhutangas listed there is deliberately not stated.
Trapdoor claim that the word dhutanga does not appear in SN 16.5: confirm (the sutta lists the practices without the collective term, as far as the writer knows).
howItsDone mentions the Thai forest tradition; confirm phrasing.
Editor: smoothed the garbled close of the teach ('can find the path still walked' to 'can see that the path is still walked').
